content: Etravirine is used in combination with at least two additional antiretroviral agents to treat HIV-1 infection in treatment-experienced patients who exhibit viral replication and documented resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). The recommended dosage is 200 mg orally every 12 hours. No dosage adjustment is required for patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class A or B). However, pharmacokinetics have not been evaluated in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class C). In pediatric patients aged 2 years or older with similar treatment resistance, safety and efficacy have not been established for those under 2 years of age. Etravirine is contraindicated with certain medications due to its effects on hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism, which can lead to decreased drug levels and reduced efficacy or increased toxicity. Drug Interactions and Contraindications: 1. Artemether/lumefantrine: Etravirine decreases their levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, leading to loss of antimalarial efficacy. Co-administration is contraindicated. 2. Carbamazepine: Reduces etravirine levels via CYP2C9/10 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 3. Cariprazine: Etravirine decreases cariprazine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 4. Cobicistat: Etravirine reduces cobicistat levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 5. Doravirine: Etravirine decreases doravirine levels, potentially leading to virologic failure and resistance. Co-administration is contraindicated. 6. Efavirenz: Reduces etravirine levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 7. Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir: Etravirine reduces the efficacy of this complete HIV regimen. Co-administration is contraindicated. 8. Fosamprenavir: Etravirine increases fosamprenavir levels, and co-administration is contraindicated. 9. Indinavir: Etravirine decreases indinavir levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 10. Isavuconazonium sulfate: Etravirine reduces its levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 11. Lopinavir/ritonavir: Etravirine reduces lopinavir levels unless ritonavir is co-administered to mitigate the effect. 12. Lumacaftor/ivacaftor: Co-administration is not recommended. 13. Mavacamten: Etravirine alters its metabolism via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, leading to increased or decreased levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 14. Naloxegol: Etravirine reduces naloxegol levels, and co-administration is contraindicated. 15. Nelfinavir: Etravirine increases nelfinavir levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 16. Nevirapine: Reduces etravirine levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 17. Ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir & dasabuvir: Etravirine reduces their levels, leading to decreased efficacy. Co-administration is contraindicated. 18. Panobinostat: Etravirine reduces its levels, potentially leading to treatment failure. Co-administration is contraindicated. 19. Phenobarbital: Reduces etravirine levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 20. Prazquantel: Etravirine reduces its levels. Discontinue etravirine two weeks before starting praziquantel and resume one day after the last dose. 21. Rifampin: Reduces etravirine levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 22. Rilpivirine: Etravirine reduces rilpivirine levels, and co-administration is contraindicated. 23. St. John’s Wort: Reduces etravirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 24. Tipranavir/ritonavir: Reduces etravirine levels, leading to loss of therapeutic effect. Co-administration is contraindicated. 25. Velpatasvir: Etravirine reduces its levels, potentially leading to virologic failure. Co-administration is contraindicated. Additional Considerations: Etravirine interacts with numerous other drugs, including anticancer agents, antifungals, and antimalarials, primarily through its effects on CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism. These interactions can lead to reduced efficacy or increased toxicity of the co-administered drugs. For drugs metabolized by CYP3A4, co-administration with etravirine often necessitates avoiding the combination or using alternative therapies. In cases where co-administration is unavoidable, dose adjustments or close monitoring may be required to mitigate adverse effects or loss of efficacy. This comprehensive understanding of etravirine’s interactions is critical for optimizing HIV treatment while minimizing risks associated with drug-drug interactions.
